translations.title: Malaysias Märkte: Ein Paradies für Feinschmecker
translations.excerpt: Malaysias Märkte sind keine reinen Einkaufsorte. Nirgendwo ist die Esskultur des Landes lebendiger. Jeden Morgen beliefern die Nassmärkte Restaurants und Hawker-Stände mit frischen Zutaten.
translations.meta_title: Malaysias Märkte: Ein Leitfaden für Feinschmecker
translations.meta_description: Malaysias Märkte sind nicht nur Orte zum Einkaufen. Hier ist die Esskultur des Landes am lebendigsten. Die Nassmärkte versorgen die Restaurants und Straßenhändler jeden Morgen mit frischen Zutaten.
translations.content_markdown:
**Was man auf einem Nassmarkt essen sollte:** Im Bereich für zubereitete Speisen frühstücken die Marktstammgäste. Halten Sie Ausschau nach Ständen, an denen ältere Kunden Schlange stehen. Das sind diejenigen, die die Marktgemeinschaft seit Jahrzehnten versorgen.

Pasar Malam (Nachtmärkte) sind temporäre Märkte, die sich an einem anderen Wochentag auf einer anderen Straße aufbauen. Sie haben von etwa 16 Uhr bis 22 Uhr geöffnet. Jedes Viertel in Malaysia hat seinen eigenen Pasar-Malam-Plan.

**Fried Chicken** (ayam goreng) auf Pasar malam wird in einem Kurkuma- und Reismehl-Teig gewendet und in heißem Öl frittiert. Die Haut ist spröde knusprig. Das Fleisch bleibt saftig, weil die Frittierzeit kurz ist. Kaufen Sie ein Stück und essen Sie es im Gehen.

## Die Märkte, die man kennen sollte

Die Simply Enak Food Tours in Malaysia besuchen mehrere dieser Märkte und bringen Sie zu den Ständen, für die sich auch die Stammkunden des Marktes anstellen. Ein einheimischer Guide macht den Unterschied aus, ob man am besten Stand vorbeiläuft oder sich dort hinsetzt.

translations.title: Los mercados de Malasia: una guía gastronómica
translations.excerpt: Los mercados de Malasia no son meros lugares de compras: allí es donde la cultura gastronómica del país cobra vida. Cada mañana, los wet markets abastecen de ingredientes frescos a restaurantes y puestos callejeros.
translations.meta_title: Los mercados de Malasia: una guía para los amantes de la comida
translations.meta_description: Los mercados de Malasia no son sólo lugares para comprar. Es allí donde la cultura gastronómica del país está más viva. Los mercados húmedos abastecen cada mañana de ingredientes frescos a los restaurantes y puestos ambulantes.
translations.content_markdown:
**Qué comer en un mercado húmedo:** La sección de comida cocinada es donde los habituales del mercado desayunan. Busca los puestos que tengan colas de clientes mayores. Estos son los que han estado alimentando a la comunidad del mercado durante décadas.

Los pasar malam (mercados nocturnos) son mercados temporales que se instalan en una calle diferente cada día de la semana. Operan desde aproximadamente las 4 PM hasta las 10 PM. Cada barrio en Malasia tiene su propio horario de pasar malam.

**Pollo frito** (ayam goreng) en los pasar malam está rebozado en una masa de cúrcuma y harina de arroz y se fríe en abundante aceite. La piel es increíblemente crujiente. La carne permanece jugosa porque el tiempo de fritura es corto. Compra un trozo y cómetelo mientras caminas.

## Los mercados que debes conocer

Los tours gastronómicos Simply Enak en Malasia visitan varios de estos mercados y te llevan a los puestos por los que hacen cola los mismos habituales del mercado. Un guía local marca la diferencia entre pasar de largo el mejor puesto y sentarte en él.

translations.title: Les marchés de Malaisie : le guide du gourmand
translations.excerpt: Les marchés malaisiens ne sont pas de simples endroits où faire ses courses. C'est là que la culture culinaire du pays est la plus vivante. Chaque matin, les marchés humides approvisionnent restaurants et stands de rue en ingrédients frais.
translations.meta_title: Les marchés de Malaisie : un guide pour les gourmands
translations.meta_description: Les marchés malaisiens ne sont pas seulement des lieux de shopping. C'est là que la culture alimentaire du pays est la plus vivante. Les marchés humides approvisionnent chaque matin les restaurants et les stands de colporteurs en ingrédients frais.
translations.content_markdown:
**Que manger dans un marché humide :** La section des plats préparés est l'endroit où les habitués du marché prennent leur petit-déjeuner. Cherchez les stands qui ont des files d'attente de clients plus âgés. Ce sont ceux qui nourrissent la communauté du marché depuis des décennies.

Les pasar malam (marchés de nuit) sont des marchés temporaires qui s'installent dans une rue différente chaque jour de la semaine. Ils fonctionnent d'environ 16h à 22h. Chaque quartier de Malaisie a son propre programme de pasar malam.

**Le poulet frit** (ayam goreng) dans les pasar malam est enrobé d'une pâte à base de curcuma et de farine de riz, puis frit dans l'huile bien chaude. La peau est extrêmement croustillante. La viande reste juteuse car le temps de friture est court. Achetez un morceau et mangez-le en marchant.

## Les marchés à connaître

Les visites gastronomiques Simply Enak en Malaisie passent par plusieurs de ces marchés et vous emmènent aux étals pour lesquels les habitués font eux-mêmes la queue. Un guide local fait toute la différence entre passer devant le meilleur étal et s'y attabler.

translations.title: De markten van Maleisië: een gids voor fijnproevers
translations.excerpt: De Maleisische markten zijn niet alleen plekken om te winkelen. Hier leeft de eetcultuur van het land het meest. De natte markten voorzien de restaurants en kraampjes elke ochtend van verse ingrediënten.
translations.meta_title: De markten van Maleisië: een gids voor fijnproevers
translations.meta_description: De Maleisische markten zijn niet alleen plekken om te winkelen. Hier leeft de eetcultuur van het land het meest. De natte markten voorzien de restaurants en kraampjes elke ochtend van verse ingrediënten.
translations.content_markdown:
**Wat je op een natte markt kunt eten:** Het gedeelte met bereid voedsel is waar de vaste marktgangers ontbijten. Zoek de kraampjes op waar rijen oudere klanten staan. Dit zijn de kraampjes die de marktgemeenschap al tientallen jaren voeden.

Pasar malam (nachtmarkten) zijn tijdelijke markten die op een andere straat opzetten, afhankelijk van de dag van de week. Ze zijn geopend van ongeveer 16 uur tot 22 uur. Elke buurt in Maleisië heeft zijn eigen pasar malam-rooster.

**Gebakken kip** (ayam goreng) op pasar malam wordt gepaneerd in een beslag van kurkuma en rijstemeel en gefrituurd in hete olie. De korst is keihard knapperig. Het vlees blijft sappig omdat de frituurtijd kort is. Koop een stuk en eet het terwijl je loopt.

## De markten om te kennen

De Simply Enak food tours in Maleisië bezoeken verschillende van deze markten en brengen je naar de kraampjes waar de vaste marktgangers zelf voor in de rij staan. Een lokale gids maakt het verschil tussen voorbijlopen aan het beste kraampje en er plaatsnemen.

translations.title: Рынки Малайзии: Путеводитель для гурманов
translations.excerpt: Рынки Малайзии, это не просто места для покупок. Именно здесь культура питания страны наиболее жива. Влажные рынки каждое утро снабжают рестораны и лотки свежими ингредиентами.
translations.meta_title: Рынки Малайзии: Путеводитель для гурманов
translations.meta_description: Рынки Малайзии, это не просто места для покупок. Именно здесь культура питания страны наиболее жива. Влажные рынки каждое утро снабжают рестораны и лотки свежими ингредиентами.
translations.content_markdown:
**Что есть на мокром рынке:** В секции готовой еды завтракают постоянные покупатели рынка. Обращайте внимание на лавки, у которых выстраиваются очереди из пожилых клиентов. Именно они на протяжении десятилетий кормят местное сообщество.

Pasar malam (ночные рынки), это временные рынки, которые разворачиваются на разных улицах в разные дни недели. Они работают примерно с 16:00 до 22:00. У каждого района Малайзии свой график работы pasar malam.

**Жареная курица** (айям горенг) на пасар-малам покрыта кляром из куркумы и рисовой муки и обжарена во фритюре. Корочка хрустит так, что ломается. Мясо остаётся сочным, потому что время жарки короткое. Купите кусочек и ешьте на ходу.

## Рынки, которые стоит знать

Гастрономические туры Simply Enak в Малайзии посещают несколько из этих рынков и приводят вас к тем лоткам, за которыми выстраиваются в очередь сами постоянные посетители рынка. Местный гид, это разница между тем, чтобы пройти мимо лучшего лотка, и тем, чтобы сесть за него.

translations.title: マレーシアの市場: グルメ愛好家のためのガイド
translations.excerpt: マレーシアのマーケットは買い物をするだけの場所ではありません。この国の食文化が最も息づく場所です。生鮮市場では、レストランや行商の屋台に毎朝新鮮な食材が供給されます。
translations.meta_title: マレーシアの市場: グルメ愛好家のためのガイド
translations.meta_description: マレーシアのマーケットは買い物をするだけの場所ではありません。この国の食文化が最も息づく場所です。生鮮市場では、レストランや行商の屋台に毎朝新鮮な食材が供給されます。
translations.content_markdown:
**ウェットマーケットで食べるべきもの：** 調理済み食品のセクションは、市場の常連客が朝食をとる場所です。年配の客が列を作っている出店を探してみてください。何十年にもわたって市場のコミュニティに食事を提供し続けているお店です。

パサール・マラム（夜市）は、曜日ごとに異なる通りに設営される一時的な市場だ。営業時間は午後4時頃から午後10時頃まで。マレーシアの各地域には、それぞれ独自のパサール・マラムのスケジュールがある。

パサール・マラムの**フライドチキン**（アヤム・ゴレン）は、ターメリックと上新粉の衣をまとわせ、深い油で揚げる。皮はぱりっぱりに揚がる。揚げる時間が短いため、肉はジューシーな状態を保っている。1切れ買って、歩きながら食べよう。

## 知っておきたい市場

マレーシアのSimply Enakフードツアーは、これらの市場のいくつかを訪れ、市場常連客が自ら並ぶ屋台へと案内してくれます。地元のガイドがいることで、最高の屋台を素通りしてしまうのと、実際に座って食事をするのとでは全く違う体験になります。

Os roteiros gastronômicos da Simply Enak na Malásia visitam vários desses mercados e levam você até as barracas pelas quais os frequentadores regulares do próprio mercado fazem fila. Um guia local faz a diferença entre passar pela melhor barraca e sentar-se nela.

title: KL Markets Worth Waking Up Early For
excerpt: A Local's Guide to KL's Markets Kuala Lumpur's markets are where the city's food culture lives. Not in the restaurants. Not in the food courts.

children.text: A Local's Guide to KL's Markets

Kuala Lumpur's markets are where the city's food culture lives. Not in the restaurants. Not in the food courts. In the wet markets, the night markets, and the covered bazaars where vendors have been selling the same goods from the same spots for decades. If you want to understand what Malaysians actually eat, you need to go to the places where they buy their ingredients.

This guide covers four markets in KL. Each serves a different purpose. One is for ingredients. One is for snacks. One is for heritage. One is for the spectacle of a thousand stalls under one roof on a Monday night.
Pudu Market: The Wet Market

Pudu Market (Pasar Pudu) is a wet market in the oldest part of KL. It opens at 5 AM and closes by 1 PM. If you arrive after 10 AM, you have missed the best stuff. The vendors have been here since before the surrounding high-rises were built, and they operate with the efficiency of people who have been doing the same job for forty years.

The market is split into sections. The produce section has the widest variety of tropical fruit you will see in KL. Dragonfruit, mangosteen, rambutan, duku, langsat, cempedak. The vendors offer samples if you look interested. Buy what is in season :  the fruit that has been flown in from other countries is rarely worth the price.

The meat section is where the term "wet market" makes sense. The floors are hosed down constantly. The chicken is slaughtered on site. The fish is displayed on ice and the vendors will gut and clean it for you in under a minute. This is not a place for the squeamish, but it is where every serious cook in KL shops.

The prepared food section is what matters for a visitor. Small stalls sell cooked food that the market vendors eat for breakfast. **Curry puff** (karipap) filled with curried potato and a slice of boiled egg. **Lemper** :  sticky rice rolls filled with spiced shredded chicken. **Kuih** :  small colourful cakes made from rice flour and coconut milk. The kuih stall at the Pudu Market entrance sells lapis legit (layered cake), kuih seri muka (pandan custard on glutinous rice), and ondeh-ondeh (glutinous rice balls filled with palm sugar and rolled in grated coconut). A piece costs RM 1. Pick three or four and you have breakfast.

**Nasi lemak** at Pudu Market is served in banana leaf packets. The sambal is made in-house and sold by the kilogram on the condiment aisle. Buy a packet to eat on the spot. The fried chicken comes from the stall next door and costs RM 3 extra.
Chow Kit Market: The Malay Food Market

Chow Kit Market (Pasar Chow Kit) is the largest Malay market in KL. It sits at the northern edge of the city centre, a sprawling complex of wet market, dry goods, and food stalls that serves the Malay community of Kuala Lumpur. The energy here is different from Pudu. Louder. More chaotic. The music is louder, the vendors call out in Malay, and the smell of fried fish and spices hits you before you reach the entrance.

The food section at the back of the market is the reason to come. Stalls sell cooked food that Malay families buy for dinner when they do not feel like cooking. The selection changes daily based on what the vendor made that morning.

**Rendang** is available from at least three different stalls. The quality varies. The rendang at the stall on the left side of the food section, run by a woman named Mak Minah, is the best. The meat is so tender it pulls apart with a fork. The sauce has reduced to a dark, oily paste that coats every piece.
**Gulai ikan** is fish curry in a turmeric and coconut milk base. The fish is cooked whole with the head on. The flesh falls off the bone. The gravy is what you want to pour over your rice.

**Sambal udang** is prawns cooked in a thick sambal that has been fried down until the oil separates. The prawns are small but the flavour is concentrated. Eat it with white rice and a handful of raw vegetables (ulam).
**Cincalok** is a fermented shrimp condiment that is specific to Malay cooking. It is sharp, salty, and works as a dip for cucumber and herbs. You can buy it by the jar at the dry goods section.

Chow Kit also sells spices by the kilogram. You can buy fresh turmeric, galangal, lemongrass, kaffir lime leaves, and belacan (dried shrimp paste) for a fraction of the supermarket price. The vendors will tell you how to use them if you ask.
Central Market: The Heritage Food Destination

Central Market (Pasar Seni) is a 1930s Art Deco building that was KL's main wet market until the 1980s. It has since been converted into a cultural centre with craft shops, art galleries, and a food court. The building itself is worth seeing :  the original structure with its high ceilings and terrazzo floors is intact.
The food court on the upper level is the draw for visitors. The stalls here are curated for the tourist market, but several of them are run by the same families who operated in the original market.

**Hainanese chicken rice** at the Central Market food court is solid. The chicken is poached, the rice is cooked in chicken fat and pandan juice, and the chilli sauce is made fresh. The stall on the far left has the longest queue.

**Ikan bakar** (grilled fish) from the Malay stall in the middle section comes wrapped in banana leaf with a sambal paste stuffed inside the fish. The flesh is moist from the banana leaf, and the sambal has cooked into the meat.

**ABC** (Air Batu Campur) is shaved ice with a mountain of toppings: red beans, sweet corn, grass jelly, cendol, peanuts, and evaporated milk. The ABC stall at Central Market serves it in a tall glass with a scoop of ice cream on top. It is not subtle. It is the most refreshing thing you will eat on a hot KL afternoon.

**Kaya toast** and **kopi-o** at the kopitiam (coffee shop) on the ground floor is a good pit stop. The toast is grilled over charcoal, spread with coconut kaya jam and cold butter. The kopi-o is strong, sweetened with condensed milk, and served in a ceramic cup with a saucer. The coffee shop has been in this building since the 1970s.
Taman Connaught Night Market: The Longest Market in KL

Taman Connaught is a residential neighbourhood in Cheras, east of the city centre. Every Monday evening, its main road transforms into what is often called the longest night market in Malaysia. Over a thousand stalls line both sides of the road for over two kilometres. It starts at 5 PM and runs until midnight.

This is a pasar malam (night market) in the Malaysian tradition. It sells everything: fresh produce, cooked food, clothes, household goods, electronics, toys, plants, and pets. The food section is concentrated in the first five hundred metres and scattered throughout the rest.

**Char kway teow** here is cooked over a portable wok station mounted on the back of a pickup truck. The cook has been doing this every Monday for fifteen years. The noodles are darker than the restaurant version, with more soy sauce and a heavier hit of chilli.

**Lok lok** is a self-service street food concept. You pick skewers of fish balls, tofu, squid, sausages, and vegetables from a refrigerated display, and the vendor boils or deep-fries them for you. You eat them with a shared pot of dipping sauce at the table. It is social, cheap, and the variety is overwhelming. A skewer costs RM 1.50.

**Grilled corn** is a night market staple. The corn is grilled in its husk over charcoal, then peeled, brushed with butter, salt, and chilli powder, and served on a stick. The smoky sweetness is the best snack you can eat while walking.

**Cendol** at Taman Connaught is made to order. The ice is shaved by a machine that looks like it was built in the 1960s. The coconut milk is poured over the top. The gula melaka is drizzled from a height. RM 3.
How to Shop at KL Markets
Bring cash. Small notes. RM 50 in notes of RM 1, RM 5, and RM 10 will cover a serious eating session at any market. Most vendors do not accept cards.
Go early. Wet markets peak between 7 AM and 9 AM. Night markets peak between 7 PM and 9 PM. The best food sells out first.
Do not be afraid to point. Not every vendor speaks English. Pointing at what you want and holding up fingers for quantity is standard practice.
Bring a reusable bag. Malaysian markets have been reducing plastic bag usage, and many vendors charge extra for plastic or do not offer it at all.

Markets are where KL food culture is most alive. The Simply Enak market tours visit Pudu Market and Chow Kit Market with a local guide who knows the vendors by name, the produce by season, and the best kuih stall in each market.

translations.excerpt: Pasar Kuala Lumpur adalah tempat tinggal budaya makanan di bandar ini. Bukan di restoran. Bukan di medan selera. Di pasar basah, pasar malam, dan bazar berbumbung tempat penjual telah s
translations.content_markdown:
Pasar ini dibahagikan kepada beberapa bahagian. Bahagian hasil mempunyai pelbagai jenis buah tropika paling luas yang akan anda lihat di KL. Buah naga, manggis, rambutan, duku, langsat, cempedak. Para penjaja menawarkan sampel jika anda kelihatan berminat. Beli apa yang sedang bermusim : buah yang diterbangkan masuk dari negara lain jarang berbaloi dengan harganya.

## Pasar Chow Kit: Pasar Makanan Melayu

**Sambal udang** ialah udang yang dimasak dalam sambal tebal yang telah digoreng sehingga minyak terpisah. Udangnya kecil tetapi rasanya pekat. Makan dengan nasi putih dan segenggam sayuran mentah (ulam).

**Ikan bakar** dari gerai Melayu di bahagian tengah dibalut dengan daun pisang dengan pes sambal disumbat ke dalam ikan. Isinya lembap kerana daun pisang, dan sambal telah masak sebati dengan daging ikan.

Ini ialah pasar malam dalam tradisi Malaysia. Ia menjual pelbagai barang: hasil segar, makanan masak, pakaian, barangan rumah, elektronik, mainan, pokok, dan haiwan peliharaan. Bahagian makanan tertumpu dalam lima ratus meter pertama dan bertaburan di sepanjang selebihnya.

Pergi awal. Pasar basah paling sibuk antara pukul 7 pagi dan 9 pagi. Pasar malam paling sibuk antara pukul 7 malam dan 9 malam. Makanan terbaik sold out dahulu.

Pasar adalah tempat budaya makanan KL paling hidup. Lawatan pasaran Simply Enak melawati Pasar Pudu dan Pasar Chow Kit dengan pemandu tempatan yang mengenali peniaga dengan nama, hasil mengikut musim, dan gerai kuih terbaik di setiap pasar.

translations.title: 吉隆坡市场本地游玩指南
translations.excerpt: 想感受吉隆坡的饮食文化，得去它的市场。不是餐馆，不是美食广场，而是菜市场、夜市和大棚集市,, 那里的摊贩一代代传承着...
translations.meta_title: 吉隆坡市场当地人指南
translations.meta_description: 吉隆坡的市场是这座城市饮食文化的发源地。不在餐馆里。不在美食广场。在菜市场、夜市和有顶棚的集市上，小贩们都在
translations.content_markdown:
市场分为几个区域。蔬果区的热带水果种类是吉隆坡最齐全的：火龙果、山竹、红毛丹、杜古、兰撒果、尖不辣。只要你表现出兴趣，商贩都会让你试吃。买当季水果吧,, 从其他国家空运来的水果通常不值那个价。

## Chow Kit 市场：马来美食市集

**参巴虾（Sambal udang）** 是用浓稠的参巴酱烹制的虾，参巴酱已炒至出油分离。虾虽小，但味道浓郁。配白饭和一把生菜（ulam）一起吃。

中间区域马来摊位的 **Ikan bakar**（烤鱼）用香蕉叶包裹,鱼肚内塞满了 sambal 酱。鱼肉因香蕉叶而保持湿润,sambal 酱的味道已经渗入肉中。

这是马来西亚传统意义上的巴刹马兰（pasar malam，即夜市）。这里应有尽有：新鲜农产品、熟食、衣物、日用品、电子产品、玩具、植物以及宠物。美食区集中在前五百米，其余部分则散布于整条街道。

早点去。湿货市场的高峰期是早上 7 点到 9 点。夜市的高峰期是晚上 7 点到 9 点。最好的食物总是最先售罄。

市场是吉隆坡（KL）饮食文化最鲜活的地方。Simply Enak 市场美食之旅会带您前往半山芭市场（Pudu Market）和秋杰市场（Chow Kit Market），由熟悉每位摊主、应季食材以及每个市场里最佳马来糕（kuih）摊位的本地向导带领游览。

translations.title: Kuala Lumpurs Märkte: Ein lokaler Guide
translations.excerpt: Kuala Lumpurs Märkte sind der Ort, an dem die Esskultur der Stadt zu Hause ist. Nicht in den Restaurants. Nicht in den Food-Courts. Sondern auf den Nassmärkten, den Nachtmärkten und in den überdachten Basaren, dort, wo Händler seit jeher
translations.meta_title: Ein lokaler Leitfaden zu den Märkten von KL
translations.meta_description: Auf den Märkten von Kuala Lumpur lebt die Esskultur der Stadt weiter. Nicht in den Restaurants. Nicht in den Food-Courts. Auf den Nassmärkten, den Nachtmärkten und den überdachten Basaren, auf denen Verkäufer tätig waren
translations.content_markdown:
Der Markt ist in Abschnitte unterteilt. Der Obst- und Gemüsebereich bietet die größte Vielfalt an tropischen Früchten, die du in KL sehen wirst. Drachenfrucht, Mangostane, Rambutan, Duku, Langsat, Cempedak. Die Verkäufer bieten dir Kostproben an, wenn du interessiert wirkst. Kaufe, was gerade Saison hat, Früchte, die aus anderen Ländern eingeflogen werden, sind selten den Preis wert.

## Chow-Kit-Markt: Der malaysische Lebensmittelmarkt

**Sambal udang** sind Garnelen, die in einer dicken Sambal zubereitet werden, die so lange gebraten wurde, bis sich das Öl absetzt. Die Garnelen sind klein, aber der Geschmack ist konzentriert. Iss es mit weißem Reis und einer Handvoll rohem Gemüse (Ulam).

**Ikan bakar** (gegrillter Fisch) vom malaiischen Stand im mittleren Abschnitt wird in Bananenblatt eingewickelt mit einer Sambal-Paste, die in den Fisch gestopft wird, serviert. Das Fleisch ist durch das Bananenblatt saftig, und die Sambal ist in das Fleisch eingekocht.

Dies ist ein Pasar Malam (Nachtmarkt) in malaysischer Tradition. Er verkauft alles: frische Produkte, gekochtes Essen, Kleidung, Haushaltswaren, Elektronik, Spielzeug, Pflanzen und Haustiere. Der Essensbereich konzentriert sich auf die ersten fünfhundert Meter und verteilt sich über den Rest.

Gehen Sie früh. Nassmärkte haben ihren Höhepunkt zwischen 7 und 9 Uhr morgens. Nachtmärkte haben ihren Höhepunkt zwischen 7 und 9 Uhr abends. Das beste Essen verkauft sich zuerst.

Märkte sind der Ort, an dem die kulinarische Kultur von KL am lebendigsten ist. Die Simply Enak Markttouren besuchen den Pudu Market und den Chow Kit Market mit einem lokalen Guide, der die Verkäufer beim Namen kennt, die Produkte nach Saison und den besten Kuih-Stand auf jedem Markt.

translations.title: Guía local de los mercados de KL
translations.excerpt: Los mercados de Kuala Lumpur son donde realmente vive la cultura gastronómica de la ciudad. No en los restaurantes. No en los patios de comidas. En los mercados húmedos, los mercados nocturnos y los bazares cubiertos donde los vendedores llevan
translations.meta_title: Una guía local de los mercados de KL
translations.meta_description: Los mercados de Kuala Lumpur son el lugar donde vive la cultura gastronómica de la ciudad. No en los restaurantes. No en los patios de comidas. En los mercados húmedos, los mercados nocturnos y los bazares cubiertos donde los vendedores han sido s
translations.content_markdown:
El mercado está dividido en secciones. La sección de productos frescos tiene la mayor variedad de frutas tropicales que verás en KL. Pitahaya, mangostán, rambután, duku, langsat, cempedak. Los vendedores ofrecen muestras si pareces interesado. Compra lo que esté de temporada: la fruta que ha sido traída en avión desde otros países rara vez vale el precio.

## Chow Kit Market: El Mercado de Comida Malaya

**Sambal udang** son gambas cocinadas en un sambal espeso que se ha fritado hasta que el aceite se separa. Las gambas son pequeñas pero el sabor es concentrado. Cómelo con arroz blanco y un puñado de verduras crudas (ulam).

El **ikan bakar** (pescado a la parrilla) del puesto malayo en la sección central viene envuelto en hoja de plátano con una pasta de sambal rellenada dentro del pescado. La carne está húmeda por la hoja de plátano, y el sambal se ha cocinado dentro de la carne.

Este es un pasar malam (mercado nocturno) en la tradición malaya. Vende de todo: productos frescos, comida preparada, ropa, artículos para el hogar, electrónica, juguetes, plantas y mascotas. La sección de comida se concentra en los primeros quinientos metros y se distribuye a lo largo del resto.

Ve temprano. Los mercados húmedos tienen su pico entre las 7 AM y las 9 AM. Los mercados nocturnos tienen su pico entre las 7 PM y las 9 PM. La mejor comida se agota primero.

Los mercados son el lugar donde la cultura gastronómica de KL cobra más vida. Los tours de mercado de Simply Enak visitan el Mercado de Pudu y el Mercado de Chow Kit con un guía local que conoce a los vendedores por su nombre, los productos de temporada y el mejor puesto de kuih en cada mercado.

translations.title: Les marchés de KL: le guide d'un local
translations.excerpt: Les marchés de Kuala Lumpur, c'est là que bat le cœur de la culture culinaire de la ville. Pas dans les restaurants. Pas dans les food courts. Dans les wet markets, les night markets et les bazars couverts où les vendeurs officient depuis des générations.
translations.meta_title: Un guide local sur les marchés de KL
translations.meta_description: Les marchés de Kuala Lumpur sont le lieu où vit la culture culinaire de la ville. Pas dans les restaurants. Pas dans les aires de restauration. Dans les marchés humides, les marchés nocturnes et les bazars couverts où les vendeurs ont été s
translations.content_markdown:
Le marché est divisé en sections. La section des produits frais offre la plus grande variété de fruits tropicaux que vous verrez à KL. Fruit du dragon, mangoustan, ramboutan, duku, langsat, cempedak. Les vendeurs proposent des échantillons si vous semblez intéressé. Achetez ce qui est de saison : les fruits importés par avion d'autres pays valent rarement leur prix.

## Marché de Chow Kit : Le marché de la nourriture malaise

**Sambal udang** est un plat de crevettes cuisinées dans un sambal épais qui a été frit jusqu'à ce que l'huile se sépare. Les crevettes sont petites mais la saveur est concentrée. Mangez-le avec du riz blanc et une poignée de légumes crus (ulam).

L'**ikan bakar** (poisson grillé) de l'échoppe malaise de la partie centrale est servi enveloppé dans une feuille de bananier avec une pâte de sambal fourrée à l'intérieur du poisson. La chair reste moelleuse grâce à la feuille de bananier, et le sambal a cuit à l'intérieur de la viande.

C'est un pasar malam (marché de nuit) dans la tradition malaisienne. On y trouve de tout : produits frais, plats cuisinés, vêtements, articles ménagers, appareils électroniques, jouets, plantes et animaux de compagnie. La section de nourriture est concentrée dans les cinq cents premiers mètres et dispersée tout au long du reste.

Allez tôt. Les marchés humides atteignent leur pic entre 7h et 9h. Les marchés de nuit atteignent leur pic entre 19h et 21h. La meilleure nourriture se vend en popular.

Les marchés sont l'endroit où la culture culinaire de KL est la plus vivante. Les visites de marché Simply Enak visitent le marché de Pudu et le marché de Chow Kit avec un guide local qui connaît les vendeurs par leur nom, les produits de saison, et le meilleur stand de kuih dans chaque marché.

translations.title: Een lokale gids voor de markten van KL
translations.excerpt: De markten van Kuala Lumpur zijn de plek waar de eetcultuur van de stad leeft. Niet in de restaurants. Niet in de foodcourts. Op de natte markten, de nachtmarkten en de overdekte bazaars waar verkopers zijn geweest
translations.meta_title: Een lokale gids voor de markten van KL
translations.meta_description: De markten van Kuala Lumpur zijn de plek waar de eetcultuur van de stad leeft. Niet in de restaurants. Niet in de foodcourts. Op de natte markten, de nachtmarkten en de overdekte bazaars waar verkopers zijn geweest
translations.content_markdown:
De markt is opgedeeld in secties. De groente- en fruitsectie heeft de grootste variatie aan tropisch fruit die je in KL zult zien. Drakenfruit, mangosteen, rambutan, duku, langsat, cempedak. De verkopers bieden proevertjes aan als je geïnteresseerd lijkt. Koop wat in het seizoen is : het fruit dat vanuit andere landen is ingevlogen is zelden de prijs waard.

## Chow Kit Market: De Maleisische Voedselmarkt

**Sambal udang** zijn garnalen gekookt in een dikke sambal die zo lang is gebakken tot de olie zich afscheidt. De garnalen zijn klein maar de smaak is geconcentreerd. Eet het met witte rijst en een handvol rauwe groenten (ulam).

**Ikan bakar** (gegrilde vis) van de Maleisische kraam in het middengedeelte komt gewikkeld in bananenblad met een sambalpasta in de vis gestopt. Het vlees is vochtig van het bananenblad, en de sambal is in het vlees getrokken.

Dit is een pasar malam (nachtmarkt) in de Maleisische traditie. Er wordt van alles verkocht: verse producten, gekookt eten, kleding, huishoudelijke artikelen, elektronica, speelgoed, planten en huisdieren. Het foodgedeelte is geconcentreerd in de eerste vijfhonderd meter en verspreid over de rest.

Ga vroeg. Natte markten pieken tussen 7 uur 's ochtends en 9 uur 's ochtends. Avondmarkten pieken tussen 7 uur 's avonds en 9 uur 's avonds. Het beste eten is het eerst uitverkocht.

Markten zijn waar de KL-eetcultuur het meest levendig is. De Simply Enak markttours bezoeken Pudu Market en Chow Kit Market met een lokale gids die de verkopers bij naam kent, de producten bij seizoen, en de beste kuih-kraam op elke markt.

translations.title: Путеводитель для местных жителей по рынкам KL
translations.excerpt: Рынки Куала-Лумпура, это место, где живет культура питания города. Не в ресторанах. Не в фуд-кортах. На мокрых рынках, ночных рынках и крытых базарах, где продавцов
translations.meta_title: Путеводитель для местных жителей по рынкам KL
translations.meta_description: Рынки Куала-Лумпура, это место, где живет культура питания города. Не в ресторанах. Не в фуд-кортах. На мокрых рынках, ночных рынках и крытых базарах, где продавцов
translations.content_markdown:
Рынок разделён на секции. В овощно-фруктовой секции представлен самый широкий ассортимент тропических фруктов, который вы увидите в Куала-Лумпуре. Питахайя, мангостан, рамбутан, дуку, лангсат, чемпедак. Торговцы предлагают попробовать фрукты, если вы проявляете интерес. Покупайте сезонные фрукты: фрукты, привезённые из других стран, редко стоят своих денег.

## Рынок Чоу Кит: малайский продуктовый рынок

**Самбал уданг**, креветки, приготовленные в густом самбале, обжаренном до тех пор, пока масло не начнёт отделяться. Креветки мелкие, но вкус концентрированный. Ешьте с белым рисом и горстью сырых овощей (улам).

**Ikan bakar** (рыба на гриле) из малайского ларька в центральной части подаётся завёрнутой в банановый лист с пастой самбал, начинённой внутрь рыбы. Мясо остаётся сочным благодаря банановому листу, а самбал пропитывает его в процессе приготовления.

Это пасар-малам (ночной рынок) в малайзийской традиции. Здесь продаётся всё: свежие продукты, готовая еда, одежда, хозяйственные товары, электроника, игрушки, растения и домашние животные. Секция с едой сосредоточена в первых пятистах метрах и разбросана по всей остальной территории.

Приходите рано. Мокрые рынки наиболее оживлённые с 7:00 до 9:00 утра. Ночные рынки наиболее оживлённые с 19:00 до 21:00. Лучшая еда распродаётся первой.

Рынки, это место, где кулинарная культура Куала-Лумпура наиболее живая. Туры по рынкам Simply Enak посещают рынок Пуд и рынок Чоу Кит с местным гидом, который знает продавцов по имени, знает, какие продукты в какое время года, и знает лучший лоток с куих на каждом рынке.

translations.meta_description: クアラルンプールの市場は、この都市の食文化が息づく場所です。レストランではありません。フードコートにはありません。生鮮市場、夜市、屋台が集まる屋根付きバザールでは、
translations.content_markdown:
市場はいくつかのセクションに分かれています。農産物セクションには、KLで見られる中で最も多種多様なトロピカルフルーツがあります。ドラゴンフルーツ、マンゴスチン、ランブータン、ドゥク、ランサット、チャンペダック。興味を示せば、ベンダーは試食させてくれます。旬のものを選んでください ― 他の国から空輸されてきたフルーツは、価格に見合う価値があることはほとんどありません。

## チョウキット市場：マレー料理市場

**Sambal udang（サンバル・ウダン）** は、油が分離するまで炒めた濃厚なサンバルで調理されたエビです。エビは小ぶりですが、旨味が凝縮されています。白いご飯と生の野菜（ulam ウラム）と一緒に食べます。

中央エリアにあるマレー料理屋の**Ikan bakar（イカン・バカール／魚の丸焼き）**は、バナナの葉に包まれ、魚の内部にサンバルペーストが詰められた状態で出てきます。バナナの葉のおかげで身はしっとりとし、サンバルが肉に染み込んでいます。

ここはマレーシアの伝統的なパサマラム（夜市）です。あらゆるものを販売しています：生鮮食品、調理済みの料理、衣料品、家庭用品、電化製品、おもちゃ、植物、ペットなど。食品エリアは最初の500メートルに集中しており、その後も点在しています。

早めに。ウェットマーケットは朝7時から9時がピーク。ナイトマーケットは夜7時から9時がピーク。人気の食べ物は最初に売り切れる。

市場はKLの食文化が最も活気に満ちている場所です。Simply Enakの市場ツアーでは、業者を名前で知り、季節の農産物を熟知し、各市場で最高のクエ（伝統的な菓子）屋台を知っている地元のガイドと共にプドゥ市場とチョウキット市場を訪れます。

O mercado é dividido em seções. A seção de produtos tem a maior variedade de frutas tropicais que você verá em KL. Pitaya, mangostão, rambutã, duku, langsate, jaca-cheirosa. Os vendedores oferecem amostras se você parecer interessado. Compre o que está da estação: as frutas que foram transportadas de outros países raramente valem o preço.

## Mercado Chow Kit: O Mercado de Comida Malaia

**Sambal udang** são camarões cozinhados em um sambal espesso que foi frito até o óleo se separar. Os camarões são pequenos, mas o sabor é concentrado. Coma com arroz branco e um punhado de vegetais crus (ulam).

O **ikan bakar** (peixe grelhado) da barraca malaia na seção central vem envolto em folha de bananeira com uma pasta de sambal recheada dentro do peixe. A carne fica úmida por causa da folha de bananeira, e o sambal cozinhou na carne.

Este é um pasar malam (mercado noturno) na tradição malaia. Vende de tudo: produtos frescos, comida pronta, roupas, utensílios domésticos, eletrônicos, brinquedos, plantas e animais de estimação. A seção de comida está concentrada nos primeiros quinhentos metros e espalhada pelo restante.

Vá cedo. Os mercados molhados têm pico entre 7h e 9h. Os mercados noturnos têm pico entre 19h e 21h. A melhor comida se esgota primeiro.

Os mercados são onde a cultura gastronômica de KL está mais viva. Os passeios de mercado da Simply Enak visitam o Mercado de Pudu e o Mercado de Chow Kit com um guia local que conhece os vendedores pelo nome, os produtos da estação, e a melhor barraca de kuih em cada mercado.

title: Jain Food in Penang: How to Eat Strictly Root-Vegetable-Free
excerpt: The Jain Food Guide to Penang You have just arrived in George Town. The smells from the hawker stalls hit you at every corner.

children.text: The Jain Food Guide to Penang

You have just arrived in George Town. The smells from the hawker stalls hit you at every corner. You want to try everything. But your Jain dietary requirements mean you cannot eat most of what you see.
No onion. No garlic. No root vegetables. No animal products of any kind. In a city where belacan, lard, and garlic are standard ingredients, finding food that fits can feel impossible.

It is not impossible. Penang has a Jain community, small but established, and the Indian vegetarian restaurants in George Town understand the requirements. The options are limited. You will eat simpler meals than your travelling companions. But you will eat well.
George Town's Little India: Your Base for Jain Eating

The area around Lebuh Pasar and Lebuh Penang is George Town's Little India. This is where the Indian community shops, eats, and gathers. It is also where you find the restaurants that understand Jain dietary needs.

**Sri Ananda Bahwan** on Lebuh Penang is a vegetarian restaurant with a large menu. The kitchen can prepare Jain versions of most dishes if you request it. The staff understand the difference between "no onion as a preference" and "no onion as a dietary requirement." They have been serving the local Jain community for years.

Order the thali: a complete meal with rice, dal, vegetable curries, roti, and a sweet dish. Tell the staff you need Jain preparation. They will adjust the curries to remove onion and garlic. The dal is made without onion at the base. The vegetable curry changes daily but can be prepared Jain-style on request.

**Restoran KRSMA** on Lebuh Pasar is another option. This is a smaller restaurant with a simpler menu, but the kitchen is more flexible. The owner understands Jain requirements personally. The thosai here is made with rice and lentil batter that contains no onion or garlic. The plain thosai and the rava thosai (made with semolina) are both safe. The idli is steamed rice and lentil cakes, naturally Jain-friendly. Order them with sambar and coconut chutney. Confirm the sambar is made without onion.

**Woodlands Restaurant** on Lebuh Penang serves North Indian and South Indian vegetarian food. The menu has a separate section for Jain dishes. The paneer dishes, dal, and vegetable curries in the Jain section are prepared without onion or garlic. The naan and roti are made without these ingredients. This is one of the few restaurants in Penang where you can order from a dedicated Jain menu without explaining your requirements.
What to Order at Indian Vegetarian Restaurants

**Idli:** Steamed rice and lentil cakes. The batter is fermented and contains no onion or garlic. It is naturally Jain-friendly. Order it with sambar and coconut chutney. Confirm the sambar is onion-free.

**Plain thosai and rava thosai:** Rice and lentil crepe. The plain version and the semolina version contain no onion or garlic. The masala thosai is stuffed with potato. If you avoid root vegetables, order the plain thosai instead.
**Vada:** Deep-fried lentil doughnuts made from urad dal. At most South Indian restaurants in Penang, the vada batter contains no onion or garlic. They work for Jain eating.
**Pongal:** Savoury rice and lentil porridge seasoned with black pepper, cumin, curry leaves, and ghee. No onion, no garlic. Ask for it without ghee if you avoid dairy.
**Chapati and roti:** Unleavened flatbreads made from wheat flour and water. Naturally Jain-friendly. Ask for it dry (no ghee on the cooking surface).
**Dal tadka:** Cooked lentils. Ask for it without onion, garlic, or ghee. Most South Indian kitchens can prepare it this way.
**Plain rice with vegetable curry:** The simplest Jain meal. Rice is always safe. Ask for the vegetable curry to be prepared without onion or garlic. Most restaurants in Little India can do this.
What to Avoid

**Nasi kandar** is the most famous dish in Penang, but it is not Jain-friendly. The curries at nasi kandar stalls contain onion and garlic as a base. The serving spoons are shared across meat and vegetable dishes. Cross-contamination is guaranteed.
**Banana leaf rice** at most Indian restaurants uses ghee on the rice and onion in the vegetable curries. You would need to request Jain preparation specifically, and not all restaurants can do this.
**Roti canai** is made with ghee at Mamak stalls. The dough may contain eggs. Even vegetarian versions are rarely Jain-compatible.

**Any Chinese hawker stall** is a risk. Even 素食 (Buddhist vegetarian) stalls use onion and garlic. Only strict temple kitchens exclude the pungent roots, and these are rare in Penang's commercial 素食 scene.
**Fried snacks at pasar malam** may look vegetarian but often contain onion in the batter.
Temple Canteens: A Limited but Reliable Option

The Kek Lok Si Temple canteen in Air Itam serves vegetarian food made to Buddhist standards. Buddhist temple kitchens exclude the five pungent roots (onion, garlic, leeks, chives, spring onion). They also exclude all animal products. The canteen is a reliable option for Jain eaters, though you should confirm that no root vegetables are used in individual dishes.
The canteen serves a buffet during temple hours. Rice, stir-fried vegetables, mock meat dishes, and soups. The selection varies daily. The food is simple but safe. A plate costs around RM 5.
The Honest Truth

Jain eating in Penang is possible but limited. You will eat well at the Indian vegetarian restaurants in Little India. You will eat safely at the Kek Lok Si temple canteen. Beyond these options, you will struggle.

The cuisine that works for Jain eating in Penang is South Indian vegetarian. The cuisine that does not work is everything else. Malay food uses belacan. Chinese food uses onion and garlic. Indian-Muslim food uses onion and ghee. Even the Buddhist vegetarian food uses onion and garlic at most commercial stalls.
Private Tour Recommendation for Strict Compliance

For strict Jain compliance, a private food tour is the best approach. A local guide who understands Jain dietary requirements can take you to the restaurants that prepare food correctly and save you the effort of explaining your diet to every new vendor.

The Simply Enak team in Penang has experience with Jain dietary needs and knows which Little India vendors to visit. The guide can confirm the preparation methods, watch the cooking, and ensure your requirements are met. No translation needed, no uncertainty, just the food that actually works for you.
Bring a small card in Tamil and Malay explaining Jain requirements. It helps at restaurants where the English phrase "Jain preparation" may not be familiar to all staff.

title: Jain Food in Kuala Lumpur: How to Eat Strictly Root-Vegetable-Free
excerpt: Jain Food Guide to Kuala Lumpur (2026) You arrive in Kuala Lumpur and the first thing you need to figure out is what you can eat.

children.text: Jain Food Guide to Kuala Lumpur (2026)

You arrive in Kuala Lumpur and the first thing you need to figure out is what you can eat. Jain dietary requirements go far beyond vegetarian. No root vegetables. No onion. No garlic. No animal products of any kind. In a city where belacan, lard, and garlic are standard ingredients, finding food that fits can feel impossible.
It is not impossible. KL has a Jain community that has been here for generations, and the neighbourhoods where they live and eat are the same places where you will find the food that works for you.
Why Kuala Lumpur Works for Jain Eating

Malaysia's Indian community has deep roots in Jain traditions. South Indian vegetarian cooking in this country shares many principles with Jain cooking: plant-based, no eggs, no meat, and a strong emphasis on sattvic ingredients. The difference is that standard South Indian vegetarian cooking uses onion and garlic freely. Jain cooking does not.

The good news is that several Indian vegetarian restaurants in KL understand Jain requirements and prepare Jain versions of their dishes. The vendors know the difference between "no onion" as a preference and "no onion" as a dietary requirement. They take it seriously because they have been serving the Jain community for decades.
Brickfields: The Centre of Jain-Friendly Food

Brickfields is where KL's Indian community is concentrated. The area around the Sri Mahamariamman Temple has the highest density of Indian vegetarian restaurants in the city. This is where you will find vendors who practise Jain cooking every day.

**Krishna Kanteen** on Jalan Tun Sambanthan has been serving Indian vegetarian food for years. The kitchen can prepare Jain versions of most dishes if you ask. The staff understands the requirements: no onion, no garlic, no root vegetables, no animal products. Order the thali, a complete meal with rice, dal, vegetable curries, roti, and a sweet dish. Tell them you need Jain preparation and they will adjust the curries accordingly.

**Saravanaa Bhavan** is a chain, but in KL it operates with the same standards as its outlets in India. They have a separate Jain menu section. The dosa, idli, and vada are all prepared without onion or garlic in the batter. The sambar is onion-free. This is one of the few places in KL where you can order confidently without explaining your requirements to a new person every time.

**Restoran Ananda Bhavan** on Jalan Tun Sambalong has a large menu with items that work for Jain eaters. The putu mayam (rice noodles with coconut and palm sugar), the thosai, and the plain idli are all naturally Jain-compatible. The rice dishes require a conversation about ghee and onion, but the restaurant is accustomed to these questions.
What to Order at Indian Vegetarian Restaurants

**Idli** is steamed rice and lentil cakes. The batter is fermented, but at South Indian restaurants it contains no onion or garlic. It is naturally Jain-friendly. Order it with sambar and coconut chutney. Confirm the sambar is made without onion.

**Thosai** is rice and lentil crepe. The plain thosai and the rava thosai are both made without onion or garlic. The masala thosai is stuffed with potato, which means it contains a root vegetable. If you follow Jain practices that exclude root vegetables, order the plain thosai instead.
**Vada** is deep-fried lentil doughnuts. They are made from urad dal and are naturally onion-free at most South Indian restaurants. They work for Jain eating.
**Pongal** is a savoury rice and lentil porridge. It is seasoned with black pepper, cumin, curry leaves, and ghee. If you avoid ghee, ask for it without. The dish contains no onion or garlic.
**Upma** is a savoury semolina porridge. It sometimes contains onion. Ask before ordering.
**Dal tadka** is cooked lentils. Ask for it without onion, garlic, or ghee. Most South Indian kitchens can prepare it this way.
**Roti** and **chapati** are unleavened flatbreads. They are made from wheat flour and water. They are naturally Jain-friendly. The cooking fat could be ghee. Ask for it dry.
What to Avoid
**Biryani** at most Indian Muslim restaurants contains meat, ghee, and onion. It is not Jain-friendly.

**Nasi kandar** is rice with mixed curries. The curries at Mamak stalls contain onion, garlic, and often meat or seafood. The vegetable curries may contain ghee. The cross-contamination risk from serving spoons is high.
**Roti canai** is made with ghee at most Mamak stalls. The dough may contain eggs at some places. Even vegetarian versions are rarely Jain-compatible.
**Banana leaf rice** at standard Indian restaurants uses ghee on the rice and onion in the vegetable curries. You would need to request Jain preparation specifically.

**Any Chinese Buddhist vegetarian stall** is often a good option for vegans, but Chinese vegetarian cooking uses onion, garlic, and leeks. The five pungent roots are excluded only in strict temple kitchens, not in commercial 素食 stalls.
Temple Canteens: A Reliable Option

The temple canteens in KL operate under stricter rules than commercial restaurants. The Sri Mahamariamman Temple at Jalan Tun H S Lee runs a canteen that serves vegetarian food prepared according to temple standards. The food is simple, fresh, and made without onion or garlic in many dishes.

The Dharma Realm Guan Yin Sagely Monastery on Jalan Ampang is a Buddhist temple with a large canteen. Buddhist temple kitchens exclude the five pungent roots (onion, garlic, leeks, chives, spring onion). They also exclude all animal products. The canteen is a reliable option for Jain eaters, though you should confirm that no root vegetables are used in individual dishes.
How to Communicate Your Requirements

The most useful phrase to learn: "Saya Jain. Tidak makan bawang, tidak makan bawang putih, tidak makan sayur dari dalam tanah." (I am Jain. I do not eat onion, I do not eat garlic, I do not eat vegetables from the ground.)

At Indian vegetarian restaurants, lead with "Jain preparation" rather than listing every ingredient. The vendor will understand what you mean. They may ask if you want "no onion no garlic" or "strict Jain" depending on whether root vegetables are part of your practice.
If you carry a small card or note in Tamil and Malay explaining Jain dietary requirements, it helps. Several restaurants in Brickfields are used to seeing these cards from the local Jain community.
The Bottom Line

KL is not a city where Jain eating is easy without local knowledge. But in the right neighbourhoods, with the right vendors, you can eat properly. Brickfields is your base. The Indian vegetarian restaurants there have been serving the Jain community for decades. They know what to do.

A local guide who understands Jain requirements can take you to the stalls that prepare food correctly and save you the effort of explaining your diet to every new vendor. The Simply Enak team in Kuala Lumpur has experience with Jain dietary needs and knows which Brickfields vendors to visit.

**Biryani** di kebanyakan restoran Muslim India mengandungi daging, ghee, dan bawang. Ia tidak mesra Jain.

"The dough may contain eggs at some places" = "Doh mungkin mengandungi telur di sesetengah tempat" - correct.

Seorang pemandu pelancong tempatan yang memahami keperluan Jain boleh membawa anda ke gerai-gerai yang menyediakan makanan dengan betul dan menjimatkan usaha anda untuk menjelaskan diet anda kepada setiap penjaja baharu. ## Brickfields：耆那教友好餐饮的中心

## 印度素食餐厅点单指南

大多数印度穆斯林餐厅的 **Biryani** 含有肉类、酥油和洋葱。它不适合耆那教饮食。

位于 J​alan Ampang 的法界观音圣寺（Dharma Realm Guan Yin Sagely Monastery）是一座佛教寺庙，拥有一个大型食堂。佛教寺庙的厨房排除五辛（洋葱、大蒜、韭菜、细香葱、青葱）。他们也排除所有动物制品。该食堂是耆那教饮食者的可靠选择，但您应确认个别菜肴中未使用根茎类蔬菜。

一位了解耆那教饮食要求的当地向导可以带您去那些能正确准备食物的摊位，省去您向每家新商家解释饮食偏好的麻烦。Simply Enak 吉隆坡团队在耆那教饮食需求方面经验丰富，知道该去 Brickfields（吉隆坡小印度）的哪些商家。

## Brickfields: Das Zentrum Jain-freundlicher Küche

## Was man in indischen vegetarischen Restaurants bestellen sollte

**Biryani** enthält in den meisten indisch-muslimischen Restaurants Fleisch, Ghee und Zwiebeln. Es ist nicht Jain-freundlich.

Das Kloster Dharma Realm Guan Yin Sagely Monastery an der Jalan Ampang ist ein buddhistischer Tempel mit einer großen Kantine. Buddhistische Tempelküchen schließen die fünf scharfen Wurzeln (Zwiebel, Knoblauch, Lauch, Schnittlauch, Frühlingszwiebel) aus. Sie schließen auch alle tierischen Produkte aus. Die Kantine ist eine verlässliche Option für Jain-Esser, obwohl Sie bestätigen sollten, dass keine Wurzelgemüse in einzelnen Gerichten verwendet werden.

Ein lokaler Guide, der die Jain-Anforderungen versteht, kann Sie zu den Ständen führen, die das Essen korrekt zubereiten, und Ihnen die Mühe ersparen, jedem neuen Anbieter Ihre Ernährungsweise erklären zu müssen. ## Qué pedir en los restaurantes vegetarianos indios

**Biryani** en la mayoría de los restaurantes indios musulmanes contiene carne, ghee y cebolla. No es apto para la alimentación jainista.

El Monasterio Budista Dharma Realm Guan Yin Sagely en Jalan Ampang es un templo budista con un comedor grande. Las cocinas de los templos budistas excluyen las cinco raíces pungentes (cebolla, ajo, puerros, cebollinos, cebolla de verdeo). También excluyen todos los productos de origen animal. ## Брикфилдс: центр джайнской еды

## Что заказывать в индийских вегетарианских ресторанах

**Бирьяни** в большинстве индийских мусульманских ресторанов содержит мясо, гхи и лук. Она не подходит для джайнов.

Монастырь Дхарма Рейл Гуань Инь Сейджли на Джалан Ампанг, буддийский храм с большой столовой. Кухни буддийских храмов исключают пять пряных кореньев (лук, чеснок, лук-порей, шнитт-лук, зелёный лук). Также исключаются все продукты животного происхождения. Столовая является надёжным вариантом для приверженцев джайнизма, хотя вам стоит уточнить, что в отдельных блюдах не используются корнеплоды.

Местный гид, который понимает джайнские требования, может отвести вас к лоткам, где еду готовят правильно, и избавит вас от необходимости объяснять свою диету каждому новому продавцу. Команда Simply Enak в Куала-Лумпуре имеет опыт работы с джайнскими диетическими потребностями и знает, к каким продавцам в Брикфилдсе стоит обратиться.

title: Heritage Food Guide Penang: Eating Through George Town
excerpt: Penang's Heritage Food Trail George Town is a UNESCO World Heritage site not because of its buildings alone.

children.text: Penang's Heritage Food Trail

George Town is a UNESCO World Heritage site not because of its buildings alone. The food is part of what earned the designation. UNESCO recognised that the living culinary traditions of Penang :  the hawker stalls, the kopitiams, the markets :  are as culturally significant as the architecture that surrounds them.

Penang's food heritage is older than Malaysia itself. It predates the colonial era in some cases, stretching back to the 18th-century trading routes that brought Chinese settlers, Indian merchants, Malay fisherfolk, and European traders to this island. Each group brought ingredients and techniques that blended into something that exists nowhere else. This guide follows the heritage trail through George Town, stopping at the stalls and shops that have been preserving these traditions for generations.
Armenian Street: The Nyonya Kitchen

Armenian Street (Lebuh Armenian) is one of the most photographed streets in George Town, famous for its mural art and heritage shophouses. But the food on this street and its surrounding lanes tells the story of Penang's Peranakan (Nyonya) culture.

The Peranakan Chinese are descendants of Chinese immigrants who married Malay locals between the 15th and 17th centuries. They developed a distinct cuisine that uses Chinese techniques with Malay ingredients. The result is food that is more fragrant, more sour, and more spice-forward than standard Chinese cooking.

**Nyonya laksa** (also called laksa lemak) is the dish that defines this cuisine. A rich coconut milk broth flavoured with lemongrass, galangal, turmeric, and chilli, poured over rice vermicelli, and topped with prawns, shredded chicken, tofu puffs, and sliced hard-boiled egg. The broth at the Nyonya laksa stall on Lorong Ikan (off Armenian Street) is made with a rempah (spice paste) that the owner grinds by hand each morning. The coconut milk is fresh, not the canned version. The sambal is served on the side so you can control the heat. RM 6.

**Otak-otak** is a Nyonya fish cake made from mackerel, coconut milk, eggs, and spices, steamed in a banana leaf parcel. The texture is soft and mousse-like, not firm like a fish cake. The stall at the junction of Armenian Street and Lebuh Pantai has been making otak-otak since the 1960s. The fish is ground by hand using a stone mortar. The spice paste includes turmeric, lemongrass, galangal, chilli, and candlenuts. Each parcel is folded in a banana leaf and grilled briefly before serving.

**Kuih** (Nyonya desserts) are sold at several shops on Armenian Street. The most famous is the kuih stall that sets up at the entrance to the Hock Teik Cheng Sin temple. The kuih lapis (layered cake) has 12 distinct layers, each steamed separately. The kuih dadar is a pandan crepe rolled around a sweet coconut filling. The kuih seri muka is a two-layer cake with a pandan custard top and glutinous rice base. RM 1.50 per piece.
Kapitan Keling Area: Indian-Muslim Heritage

The area around Kapitan Keling Mosque (Masjid Kapitan Keling) is the Muslim heart of George Town. The mosque was built in the early 1800s by Indian-Muslim traders. The food stalls around it reflect the same South Indian and Malay influences that the community brought with them.

**Nasi kandar** in Penang is different from the KL version. The curries are thinner and more liquid, designed to be poured over rice rather than eaten as a side. The selection is smaller but each curry is more carefully spiced. The nasi kandar stall on Lebuh Kapitan Keling opposite the mosque has been operating since the 1970s. The curry sauce is poured from a height, mixing the fish curry, chicken curry, and dal together as it lands on the rice. Order the fried chicken and the brinjal (eggplant) curry.

**Murtabak** is the stuffed version of roti canai. The dough is stretched thin, filled with spiced minced beef, egg, and onion, folded into a square parcel, and fried on a flat grill until golden. The murtabak at the Kapitan Keling area is made with a thinner dough than the KL version, resulting in a crispier exterior. The filling is more generously spiced, with cinnamon, cardamom, and cloves in the mince. Served with a bowl of curry for dipping. RM 5.

**Briyani** at the Kapitan Keling area is made by a stall that cooks in large copper pots over wood fire. The rice is long-grain basmati, pre-soaked, layered with marinated chicken or mutton, and sealed with dough so the steam circulates inside the pot. The result is rice that is separate, fragrant, and infused with the meat juices. The briyani here is only available on Fridays, when the Muslim community gathers for prayers and a post-mosque meal.
Clan Jetties: The Chinese Fishing Heritage

The clan jetties (pengkalan) on the Weld Quay waterfront are wooden villages built on stilts over the sea. Each jetty was settled by a different Chinese clan :  the Ong jetty, the Lim jetty, the Tan jetty, the Yeoh jetty :  whose members worked as fisherfolk and traders. The food at the jetties reflects that fishing heritage.

**Koay Teow Th'ng** (also spelled kway teow th'ng) is a clear noodle soup that originated with the Chinese fishing community. Flat rice noodles in a light, savoury broth made from pork bones and dried anchovies, topped with fish balls, sliced fish cake, and minced pork. The broth is clear, clean, and restorative :  the opposite of the heavy spice bombs that Penang is more famous for. The stall at the entrance to Chew Jetty has been serving Koay Teow Th'ng since the jetty was built in the late 19th century. The fish balls are made from Spanish mackerel that the family catches themselves.

**Char kway teow at the jetties** is different from the George Town version. The noodles are fatter. The soy sauce is lighter. The cockles are larger and served raw on top, a tradition from the days when fisherfolk ate what they caught. The stall at the end of Tan Jetty opens at 11 AM and closes when the noodles run out, usually by 2 PM.

**Cendol** near the jetties is sold from a cart that has been at the same spot on Weld Quay since the 1950s. The green jelly is made from rice flour and pandan. The coconut milk is fresh. The gula melaka is made from palm sugar sourced from Balik Pulau. The cart has no name. It is just the cendol cart at the end of the jetties.
The Kopitiams That Hold It Together

The streets between these heritage nodes are lined with kopitiams that have been operating since the early 20th century. These coffee shops are the infrastructure that holds Penang's hawker culture together. A kopitiam provides tables, chairs, and drinks. Independent hawkers rent space at the kopitiam's front counter. You order your drink from the kopitiam and your food from the hawker stall.

**Kedai Kopi Heng Huat** on Chulia Street has been operating since the 1940s. The coffee is made from beans roasted with butter and sugar, a Hainanese technique that produces a dark, slightly sweet brew. The kaya toast is made with coconut jam that the owner's wife cooks in the back kitchen. The half-boiled eggs are timed to the second.

**Sin Hup Aun Cafe** on Lebuh Cintra has been serving coffee since the 1930s. The building is a pre-war shophouse with original floor tiles and wooden shutters. The coffee is served in a ceramic cup with a saucer, the same way it has been served for 90 years. The toast is grilled over charcoal. The butter is a thick slab of cold butter that melts slowly into the warm kaya.
What Penang's Heritage Means for a First-Time Visitor

The heritage food trail of Penang is walkable. Armenian Street, Kapitan Keling, and the clan jetties are all within a 30-minute walk of each other. The distance between them is filled with kopitiams, street stalls, and small restaurants that each hold a piece of the island's food history.

The challenge is knowing which stalls are the ones with real history and which ones opened last year. The difference is not always visible. A faded sign and a handwritten menu are better indicators than a shiny Instagram caption. The stalls that have been here for generations do not need to market themselves. Their reputation is carried by the people who return to eat at them year after year.

The Simply Enak Penang heritage food tour covers Armenian Street, the Kapitan Keling area, and the clan jetties in one afternoon. A local guide who grew up in George Town walks you through each neighbourhood, introduces you to the vendors, and explains the history behind each dish.

translations.title: Jejak Makanan Warisan Pulau Pinang
translations.excerpt: George Town ialah tapak Warisan Dunia UNESCO bukan kerana bangunannya sahaja. Makanan adalah sebahagian daripada apa yang mendapat jawatan itu. UNESCO mengiktiraf bahawa tradisi kulinari hidup Pulau Pinang : the
translations.content_markdown:
Orang Cina Peranakan adalah keturunan pendatang China yang berkahwin dengan penduduk tempatan Melayu antara abad ke-15 dan ke-17. Mereka membangunkan masakan yang tersendiri yang menggunakan teknik China dengan bahan-bahan Melayu. Hasilnya ialah makanan yang lebih wangi, lebih masam, dan lebih hadapan rempahnya berbanding masakan Cina biasa.

**Kuih** (pencuci mulut Nyonya) dijual di beberapa kedai di Jalan Armenian. Yang paling terkenal ialah gerai kuih yang berniaga di pintu masuk tokong Hock Teik Cheng Sin. Kuih lapis mempunyai 12 lapisan yang berbeza, setiap satu dikukus secara berasingan. Kuih dadar adalah crepe pandan yang digulung dengan inti kelapa manis. Kuih seri muka adalah kek dua lapisan dengan lapisan atas kastard pandan dan lapisan bawah pulut. RM 1.50 sebiji.

**Murtabak** adalah versi stuffed roti canai. Dohnya diregangkan nipis, diisi dengan daging lembu cincang berempah, telur, dan bawang, dilipat menjadi peket segi empat, dan digoreng di atas panggangan rata sehingga keemasan. Murtabak di kawasan Kapitan Keling dibuat dengan doh yang lebih nipis berbanding versi KL, menghasilkan bahagian luar yang lebih rangup. Isinya lebih banyak berempah, dengan kayu manis, buah pelaga, dan cengkih dalam daging cincang. Dihidangkan dengan semangkuk kari untuk dicelup. RM 5.

**Koay Teow Th'ng** (juga dieja kway teow th'ng) ialah sup mi yang jernih yang berasal daripada komuniti memancing Cina. Mi beras rata di dalam kuah yang ringan dan sedap yang diperbuat daripada tulang babi dan ikan bilis kering, dihiasi dengan bebola ikan, hirisan kek ikan, dan daging babi cincang. Kuahnya jernih, bersih, dan menyegarkan : bertentangan dengan rempah berat yang lebih terkenal dengan Pulau Pinang. Gerai di pintu masuk Chew Jetty telah menyajikan Koay Teow Th'ng sejak jeti itu dibina pada akhir abad ke-19. Bebola ikan diperbuat daripada ikan tenggiri Sepanyol yang ditangkap sendiri oleh keluarga tersebut.

**Kedai Kopi Heng Huat** di Jalan Chulia telah beroperasi sejak tahun 1940-an. Kopi dibuat daripada biji yang disangrai bersama mentega dan gula, satu teknik Hainanes yang menghasilkan minuman yang gelap dan sedikit manis. Roti kaya dibuat dengan jem kelapa yang dimasak sendiri oleh isteri pemilik di dapur belakang. Telur separuh masak dimasak mengikut masa yang tepat.

Lawatan makanan warisan Simply Enak Penang merangkumi Armenian Street, kawasan Kapitan Keling, dan jeti puak dalam satu petang. Seorang pemandu tempatan yang membesar di George Town akan membawa anda melalui setiap kejiranan, memperkenalkan anda kepada penjual, dan menjelaskan sejarah di sebalik setiap hidangan.

translations.title: 槟城 heritage 美食路线
translations.excerpt: 乔治城被联合国教科文组织列为世界遗产，靠的不仅是建筑，美食同样是获此殊荣的关键。联合国教科文组织认可槟城生生不息的饮食传统：
translations.meta_title: 槟城传统美食之路
translations.meta_description: 乔治城被联合国教科文组织列为世界遗产，不仅仅是因为它的建筑。食物是赢得这一称号的一部分。联合国教科文组织承认槟城现存的烹饪传统：
translations.content_markdown:
土生华人是15至17世纪间与当地马来人通婚的中国移民后裔。他们发展出了一种独特的 cuisine，融合了中国的烹饪技艺和马来西亚的食材。比起标准的中餐，这种美食更加香气四溢、口感更酸、也更注重香料的使用。

**娘惹糕点**( Nyonya desserts)在亚美尼亚街的多家店铺有售。其中最负盛名的是在福德正神庙( Hock Teik Cheng Sin temple)入口处摆摊的糕点摊。千层糕( kuih lapis)共分 12 层,每层分别蒸制。班兰薄饼( kuih dadar)是以班兰叶制成的薄饼皮,卷入香甜椰丝馅料。双层糯米糕( kuih seri muka)是上下两层的糕点,上层为班兰叶卡仕达,下层为糯米底。每片马币 1.50 元。

**印度煎饼（murtabak）**是印度抛饼（roti canai）的馅料版本。面团被擀得很薄，填入加了香料的碎牛肉、鸡蛋和洋葱，折成方形小包，然后在平底锅上煎至金黄。甲必丹吉灵区的印度煎饼使用的面团比吉隆坡的版本更薄，因此外皮更酥脆。馅料的香料味更浓郁，肉末中加入了肉桂、小豆蔻和丁香。配一碗咖喱蘸食。价格5令吉。

**Koay Teow Th'ng（粿条汤）**（也拼作 kway teow th'ng）是一种源自华人渔村社区的清汤面食。扁平米粉浸在用猪骨和江鱼仔熬制的清淡鲜美汤底中，配上鱼丸、鱼片和肉末。汤头清澈、干净、滋补,, 与槟城更为人熟知的浓郁香料重口味截然相反。位于周氏码头（Chew Jetty）入口处的摊档，自 19 世纪末码头建成以来一直在供应粿条汤。鱼丸由这家人自己捕捞的西班牙鲭鱼制成。

**Kedai Kopi Heng Huat**位于 Chulia Street，自 1940 年代起便开始营业。咖啡由用黄油和糖一起烘焙的咖啡豆制成，这是海南人的工艺，酿出的咖啡颜色深且略带甜味。咖椰吐司所用的椰子酱，是店主的妻子在后厨亲手熬制的。半熟蛋的烹煮时间精确到秒。

Simply Enak 槟城文化美食之旅将在一个下午带您走遍亚美尼亚街、甲必丹吉灵区域和宗族码头。一位在乔治市土生土长的当地导游将陪同您穿街走巷,将您介绍给各个摊主,并为您讲解每道菜肴背后的历史故事。

translations.title: Penangs Heritage Food Trail
translations.excerpt: George Town ist nicht nur wegen seiner Gebäude UNESCO-Weltkulturerbe. Die lokale Küche hat wesentlich zu dieser Auszeichnung beigetragen. Die UNESCO würdigte die lebendigen kulinarischen Traditionen Penangs:
translations.meta_title: Penangs Heritage Food Trail
translations.meta_description: George Town gehört nicht nur wegen seiner Gebäude zum UNESCO-Weltkulturerbe. Das Essen ist Teil dessen, was die Auszeichnung verdient hat. Die UNESCO hat anerkannt, dass die lebendigen kulinarischen Traditionen von Penang: die
translations.content_markdown:
Die Peranakan-Chinesen sind Nachkommen chinesischer Einwanderer, die zwischen dem 15. und 17. Jahrhundert malaiische Einheimische heirateten. Sie entwickelten eine eigenständige Küche, die chinesische Techniken mit malaiischen Zutaten verbindet. Das Ergebnis ist ein Essen, das duftender, säuerlicher und würziger ist als die übliche chinesische Küche.

**Kuih** (Nyonya-Desserts) werden in mehreren Geschäften in der Armenian Street verkauft. Am bekanntesten ist der Kuih-Stand, der am Eingang des Hock Teik Cheng Sin-Tempels seine Waren anbietet. Der Kuih lapis (Schichtkuchen) hat 12 deutlich erkennbare Schichten, die jeweils einzeln gedämpft werden. Der Kuih dadar ist eine Pandan-Crêpe, die um eine süße Kokosfüllung gerollt wird. Der Kuih seri muka ist ein zweischichtiger Kuchen mit einem Pandan-Custard-Boden und einem Klebreisboden. RM 1,50 pro Stück.

**Murtabak** ist die gefüllte Version von Roti Canai. Der Teig wird dünn ausgezogen, mit gewürztem Hackfleisch, Ei und Zwiebel gefüllt, zu einem quadratischen Päckchen gefaltet und auf einer flachen Grillplatte goldbraun gebraten. Der Murtabak im Kapitan-Keling-Viertel wird mit einem dünneren Teig als die KL-Version hergestellt, was zu einer knusprigeren Außenseite führt. Die Füllung ist großzügiger gewürzt, mit Zimt, Kardamom und Nelken im Hackfleisch. Serviert mit einer Schale Curry zum Dippen. RM 5.

**Koay Teow Th'ng** (auch kway teow th'ng geschrieben) ist eine klare Nudelsuppe, die aus der chinesischen Fischergemeinschaft stammt. Flache Reisnudeln in einer leichten, würzigen Brühe aus Schweineknochen und getrockneten Sardellen, garniert mit Fischbällchen, geschnittenem Fischkuchen und Hackfleisch. Die Brühe ist klar, sauber und wohltuend : das Gegenteil der schweren Gewürzbomben, für die Penang berühmter ist. Der Stand am Eingang zum Chew-Jetty serviert seit dem Bau des Jetties Ende des 19. Jahrhunderts Koay Teow Th'ng. Die Fischbällchen werden aus spanischer Makrele hergestellt, die die Familie selbst fängt.

**Kedai Kopi Heng Huat** in der Chulia Street ist seit den 1940er Jahren in Betrieb. Der Kaffee wird aus Bohnen hergestellt, die mit Butter und Zucker geröstet werden, eine Hainanese-Technik, die einen dunklen, leicht süßen Aufguss ergibt. Der Kaya-Toast wird mit Kokoskonfitüre zubereitet, die die Frau des Besitzers in der hinteren Küche kocht. Die weichgekochten Eier werden auf die Sekunde genau timiert.

Die Simply Enak Penang Heritage Food Tour führt an einem Nachmittag durch die Armenian Street, das Kapitan-Keling-Viertel und die Clan-Jetties. Ein lokaler Guide, der in George Town aufgewachsen ist, führt Sie durch jedes Viertel, stellt Ihnen die Verkäufer vor und erklärt die Geschichte hinter jedem Gericht.

translations.excerpt: George Town es Patrimonio de la Humanidad por la UNESCO no solo por sus edificios. La gastronomía fue parte esencial de ese reconocimiento. La UNESCO entendió que las tradiciones culinarias vivas de Penang: el
translations.meta_title: Ruta gastronómica patrimonial de Penang
translations.meta_description: George Town es Patrimonio de la Humanidad por la UNESCO no sólo por sus edificios. La comida es parte de lo que le valió la designación. La UNESCO reconoció que las tradiciones culinarias vivas de Penang: el
translations.content_markdown:
Los chinos Peranakan son descendientes de inmigrantes chinos que se casaron con locales malayos entre los siglos XV y XVII. Desarrollaron una cocina distintiva que utiliza técnicas chinas con ingredientes malayos. El resultado es una comida más fragante, más ácida y con más especias que la cocina china estándar.

**Kuih** (postres Nyonya) se venden en varias tiendas de Armenian Street. El más famoso es el puesto de kuih que se instala en la entrada del templo Hock Teik Cheng Sin. El kuih lapis (pastel en capas) tiene 12 capas distintas, cada una cocinada al vapor por separado. El kuih dadar es un crepe de pandan enrollado alrededor de un relleno dulce de coco. El kuih seri muka es un pastel de dos capas con una cobertura de natilla de pandan y una base de arroz glutinoso. RM 1.50 por pieza.

**El murtabak** es la versión rellena del roti canai. La masa se estira fina, se rellena con carne de res picada especiada, huevo y cebolla, se dobla en forma de cuadrado y se fríe en una plancha hasta dorarse. El murtabak en la zona de Kapitan Keling se elabora con una masa más fina que la versión de Kuala Lumpur, lo que da como resultado un exterior más crujiente. El relleno está más generosamente especiado, con canela, cardamomo y clavos en la carne picada. Se sirve con un cuenco de curry para mojar. RM 5.

**Koay Teow Th'ng** (también escrito kway teow th'ng) es una sopa de fideos clara que se originó con la comunidad pesquera china. Fideos de arroz planos en un caldo ligero y sabroso hecho con huesos de cerdo y anchoas secas, cubierto con albóndigas de pescado, pastel de pescado en rodajas y carne de cerdo molida. El caldo es claro, limpio y reconfortante : lo opuesto a las bombas de especias pesadas por las que Penang es más famoso. El puesto en la entrada al Muelle Chew ha estado sirviendo Koay Teow Th'ng desde que el muelle fue construido a finales del siglo XIX. Las albóndigas de pescado están hechas de caballa que la familia pesca ellos mismos.

**Kedai Kopi Heng Huat** en Chulia Street ha estado operando desde la década de 1940. El café está hecho de granos tostados con mantequilla y azúcar, una técnica hainana que produce un brebaje oscuro y ligeramente dulce. La tostada con kaya está hecha con mermelada de coco que la esposa del dueño cocina en la cocina trasera. Los huevos medio hervidos se cronometran al segundo.

El tour gastronómico patrimonial Simply Enak Penang cubre Armenian Street, la zona de Kapitan Keling y los clan jetties en una tarde. Un guía local que creció en George Town te lleva por cada vecindario, te presenta a los vendedores y te explica la historia detrás de cada platillo.

translations.title: Le parcours du patrimoine gastronomique de Penang
translations.excerpt: George Town est classée au patrimoine mondial de l'UNESCO, et pas seulement pour ses bâtiments. La cuisine fait partie intégrante de ce qui lui a valu ce titre. L'UNESCO a reconnu que les traditions culinaires vivantes de Penang : la
translations.meta_title: Sentier gastronomique du patrimoine de Penang
translations.meta_description: George Town est un site du patrimoine mondial de l'UNESCO, pas seulement à cause de ses bâtiments. La nourriture fait partie de ce qui a valu cette désignation. L'UNESCO a reconnu que les traditions culinaires vivantes de Penang : la
translations.content_markdown:
Les Chinois peranakan sont les descendants d'immigrants chinois qui ont épousé des locaux malais entre le XVe et le XVIIe siècle. Ils ont développé une cuisine distincte qui utilise des techniques chinoises avec des ingrédients malais. Le résultat est une nourriture plus parfumée, plus acidulée et plus épicée que la cuisine chinoise classique.

**Les kuih** (desserts Nyonya) sont vendus dans plusieurs boutiques d'Armenian Street. Le plus célèbre est le stand de kuih qui s'installe à l'entrée du temple Hock Teik Cheng Sin. Le kuih lapis (gâteau en couches) comporte 12 couches distinctes, chacune cuite à la vapeur séparément. Le kuih dadar est une crêpe au pandan enroulée autour d'une garniture sucrée à la noix de coco. Le kuih seri muka est un gâteau à deux couches avec un flan au pandan sur le dessus et une base de riz gluant. 1,50 RM la pièce.

Le **murtabak** est la version farcie du roti canai. La pâte est étirée finement, garnie de bœuf haché épicé, d'œuf et d'oignon, pliée en un carré, puis frite sur un grill plat jusqu'à ce qu'elle soit dorée. Le murtabak du quartier de Kapitan Keling est préparé avec une pâte plus fine que la version de KL, ce qui donne un extérieur plus croustillant. La garniture est plus généreusement épicée, avec de la cannelle, de la cardamome et des clous de girofle dans la viande hachée. Servi avec un bol de curry pour tremper. RM 5.

**Koay Teow Th'ng** (aussi orthographié kway teow th'ng) est une soupe de nouilles claire qui est née de la communauté de pêcheurs chinois. Des nouilles de riz plates dans un bouillon léger et savoureux à base d'os de porc et d'anchois séchés, garnies de boulettes de poisson, de tranches de gâteau de poisson et de porc haché. Le bouillon est clair, net et réparateur : à l'opposé des bombes d'épices lourdes pour lesquelles Penang est plus connue. L'étal à l'entrée de Chew Jetty sert du Koay Teow Th'ng depuis que la jetée a été construite à la fin du 19ème siècle. Les boulettes de poisson sont fabriquées à partir de maquereau espagnol que la famille pêche elle-même.

**Kedai Kopi Heng Huat** sur Chulia Street fonctionne depuis les années 1940. Le café est préparé à partir de grains torréfiés avec du beurre et du sucre, une technique hainanaise qui produit une boisson foncée, légèrement sucrée. Le kaya toast est fait avec une confiture de coco que la femme du propriétaire cuisine dans la cuisine à l'arrière. Les œufs mollets sont cuits à la seconde près.

La visite gastronomique du patrimoine de Simply Enak Penang couvre Armenian Street, le quartier de Kapitan Keling et les jetées des clans en un après-midi. Un guide local qui a grandi à George Town vous emmène à travers chaque quartier, vous présente les vendeurs et vous explique l'histoire derrière chaque plat.
